actor: Unknown (the publisher of the npm package)
impact: Per Koi Security and Snyk, every email sent through version 1.0.16 or later was blind-copied to an attacker-controlled address. That mail could include password resets, invoices and internal correspondence. Koi estimates about 300 organisations and 3,000-15,000 emails a day were affected; no measured victim count is published.
mitigations: Postmark advises anyone who used the package to remove it immediately, check email logs for suspicious activity, rotate any credentials that may have been sent by email during the compromise period, and use only official Postmark resources.
Koi Security recommends uninstalling the package, rotating credentials sent by email, auditing email logs for unexpected BCC recipients, and auditing every MCP server in use.

Snyk recommends removing the package from all environments, blocking the exfiltration domain at egress, rotating Postmark API and SMTP credentials and any credentials that may appear in emails, and checking for other packages from the same npm publisher.
name: postmark-mcp: an npm MCP server impersonating Postmark silently BCC'd every email sent through it to an attacker

sources.title: First Malicious MCP in the Wild: The Postmark Backdoor That's Stealing Your Emails
Malicious MCP Server on npm postmark-mcp Harvests Emails
Trust in MCP takes first in-the-wild hit via squatted Postmark connector

summary: On 2025-09-25 Koi Security disclosed that postmark-mcp had been backdoored. The npm package presented itself as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI assistants send email through Postmark. In version 1.0.16 a single added line blind-copied every email sent through it to an attacker-controlled address. Koi called it the first malicious MCP server seen in the wild. The package copied code from the legitimate Postmark MCP server that Postmark (ActiveCampaign) maintains on GitHub. The same day, Postmark stated that it had nothing to do with the package, had not published its MCP server on npm, and that its API and services were unaffected. Snyk also analysed the package on 2025-09-25 and found the BCC insertion was the only notable change between benign version 1.0.15 and malicious version 1.0.18. Snyk's timeline has version 1.0.0 first published on 2025-09-15, version 1.0.18 on 2025-09-17, and the package gone from npm by 2025-09-25. Koi reported about 1,500 weekly downloads and said the publisher deleted the package without responding after Koi made contact. Installed copies keep exfiltrating until they are removed. Koi's figures of about 300 organisations and 3,000-15,000 emails a day are its own rough estimate, not a measured count. AI agent tooling was the distribution channel: assistants used the backdoored tool as normal and did not operate the attack.
